title: Bond Pricing, Yields and Yield to Maturity
objectives: Price a coupon bond by discounting each cash flow at the market yield
Define yield to maturity, explain how it is found, and state its assumptions and limits
Compute an approximate YTM from price, coupon, face and maturity and check it against the exact rate
Explain the inverse price-yield relation and discount versus premium pricing
motivation: A portfolio manager is offered a 5% coupon bond at 97.33 per 100 of face and must decide within minutes whether it is rich or cheap. Bond pricing is discounted-cash-flow arithmetic with real money attached: one slipped discount factor misprices every bond on the desk. This lesson builds the pricing equation cash flow by cash flow, then defines the yield to maturity the market quotes back from it.

blocks.text: Price is the present value of the promised cash flows

blocks.md: Strip away the jargon and a bond is just a schedule of promised payments: coupons each period and the return of principal at maturity. To value it, discount every cash flow at the rate the market currently demands for paper of that credit quality and maturity - the bond's yield. Nothing more is involved. The discipline is in the arithmetic: each coupon is discounted separately, with a compounding factor raised to that payment's time, and the price is the sum. If the discounted cash flows add to more than the quoted price the bond is cheap; if less, it is rich. Desks reprice bonds exactly this way thousands of times a day.

blocks.caption: Coupon $C_t$ paid at each date $t$, face value $F$ repaid at maturity, yield $y$ per period (annual compounding here).

blocks.md: Work one bond end to end. It matures in 3 years, pays a 5% annual coupon on \$1{,}000 face (so \$50 each year), and the market yield for comparable risk is 6% per year. Discount each cash flow at 6%:

The price sits below par (97.33 per 100 of face) because the 5% coupon is below the 6% the market demands; the price must drop until coupons plus the pull up toward par at maturity compound to exactly 6%. Reverse the logic for a premium bond: an 8% coupon when the market yields 5% prices above par. Price and quoted yield are two encodings of the same number, locked together by an inverse relation: yields go up, prices go down, always.

blocks.caption: A flat 6% curve. With a flat term structure every cash flow is discounted at one rate - exactly the single-yield setup above. Bend the curve and the single-yield shortcut starts to creak.

blocks.text: Yield to maturity: the number the market quotes

blocks.md: The **yield to maturity (YTM)** is the single discount rate that makes the discounted cash flows add up to the observed market price. It is the bond's internal rate of return: given the price and the cash-flow schedule, YTM is the $y$ that solves the pricing equation above. Unlike the price, it cannot be computed in one pass - you guess a rate, price the bond, compare with the market, and iterate until the computed price matches. Screen yields are YTMs, which is why a bond's price and its quoted yield carry identical information: quoting one determines the other.

blocks.title: YTM is an IRR, not a magic number
blocks.md: Pricing engines solve for YTM with Newton's method or bisection on the pricing function. For pencil checks, the approximation below lands within a few basis points whenever the yield is near the coupon - good enough to catch a bad quote.

blocks.caption: $C$ annual coupon, $F$ face value, $P$ price, $n$ years to maturity.

blocks.title: Approximate YTM of our bond priced at \$973.27
items: Average annual capital gain toward par: $(1000 - 973.27)/3 = 26.73/3 = 8.91$.
Denominator: average of face and price = $(1000 + 973.27)/2 = 986.64$.
The true YTM is 6.00% by construction - discounting at 6% reproduced the price. The approximation is about 3 bp off: fine for a sanity check, not for trading.

blocks.md: YTM carries assumptions worth respecting. It assumes you hold to maturity, every coupon arrives on time, and each coupon is reinvested at the YTM itself - optimistic when rates fall, because reinvestment then earns less and your realized compound return drops below the quoted YTM. It also collapses the whole term structure into one number, which is only honest on a flat curve. Sellers quote YTM because it makes bonds comparable at a glance; risk managers never stop at it, as the next lessons show.

blocks.title: Clean, dirty and compounding conventions
blocks.md: Quoted bond prices are usually **clean** prices excluding accrued interest; the invoice (dirty) price you actually pay adds interest accrued since the last coupon. Compounding conventions differ by market too: a 6% semiannual-bond yield is not the same as 6% compounded annually. Always check the convention before comparing yields across bonds or countries.

blocks.code:
face, coupon, n, y = 1000, 50, 3, 0.06
price = sum(coupon / (1 + y) ** t for t in range(1, n + 1)) + face / (1 + y) ** n
print(round(price, 2))          # 973.27
approx = (coupon + (face - price) / n) / ((face + price) / 2)
print(round(approx * 100, 2))   # 5.97
blocks.caption: Hand arithmetic first, then let the machine confirm it.

guidedExercise.prompt: A 2-year bond pays a 4% annual coupon on \$1{,}000 face and the market yield is 5%. Price the bond from its cash flows, state whether it is a discount or premium bond, and check your answer with the approximate YTM formula.
hints: Discount each cash flow separately: two coupons of \$40 and the final \$1,040.
A coupon below the yield means a price below face - use that as a sanity check.

independentExercise.prompt: A 4-year bond pays a 6% annual coupon on $1{,}000 face; the market yield is 7%. Compute the price from discounted cash flows (discount factors to six decimals), decide discount versus premium, and estimate the YTM with the approximation formula. Note $1.07^4 = 1.310796$.
hints: The coupon is below the yield, so expect a price below par.

commonMistakes: Discounting cash flows at the coupon rate instead of the market yield - the yield, not the coupon, sets the discount factors.
Forgetting the principal repayment in the final cash flow (it is coupon + face).
Treating YTM as a promised return: it assumes reinvestment of coupons at the YTM and no default.
Comparing a semiannual-compounding yield with an annual-compounding yield without converting.
realWorldApplication: Every pricing screen, OMS and risk system marks fixed-income positions by discounting scheduled cash flows; the price-yield pair printed on a bond quote is the same two-view encoding computed here.
quantFinanceApplication: The iterative YTM solve is the simplest example of root-finding on a pricing function - the same pattern later prices options via implied volatility and calibrates curve models to market quotes.
summary: A bond's price is the sum of its discounted cash flows: $P = \sum_t C_t/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^n$.
YTM is the single rate equating price to discounted cash flows - the bond's IRR - found by iteration, not direct algebra.
Coupon below yield means price below par (discount bond); coupon above yield means price above par (premium bond); price and yield move inversely.
The approximation $y \approx [C + (F-P)/n]/[(F+P)/2]$ lands within a few basis points when yield is near the coupon.
YTM assumes reinvestment at the YTM and a flat curve; realized compound returns can differ.

quiz.prompt: A bond has an 8% annual coupon and the market yield for its risk is 5%. Its price is:
options: Above par, because the coupon exceeds the required yield
Below par, because yields are high
Exactly par, because coupons are fixed
It depends on the face value
quiz.explanation: Coupon above yield means the discounted cash flows exceed face, so the price is above par (premium bond). Price and coupon/yield gap move together.

quiz.prompt: What is the present value of a \$1,000 payment due in 2 years at a 5% annual yield? (Two decimals.)
A 5-year bond with a \$40 annual coupon on \$1,000 face trades at \$950. Using the approximation formula, what is the approximate YTM in percent? (Two decimals.)
The yield to maturity implicitly assumes that interim coupons are reinvested:
options: At whatever rate prevails when each coupon arrives
quiz.explanation: YTM compounds the whole investment at one rate, which implicitly reinvests coupons at that same rate. If rates fall, realized compound return drops below the quoted YTM.

quiz.prompt: A 1-year zero-coupon bond with \$1,000 face yields 4% annually. What is its price? (Two decimals.)
quiz.explanation: $1000 / 1.04 = 961.54$. For zeros, price = face discounted once; there are no coupons.

quiz.prompt: Why does a bond's price fall when market yields rise?
options: Fixed cash flows are discounted at a higher rate, so each present value shrinks
The issuer redeems bonds early when rates rise
Coupons are cancelled when yields rise
Higher yields increase the coupon payments
quiz.explanation: Cash flows are fixed by contract; only the discount factors move. Higher $(1+y)^t$ factors shrink every PV, so the sum - the price - falls. The inverse price-yield relation is pure discounting.

flashcards.back: $P = \sum_{t=1}^{n} C_t/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^n$ - each cash flow discounted at the market yield $y$.
The single discount rate that equates a bond's market price to the present value of its cash flows; the bond's IRR. Solved by iteration.
Coupon < yield => price below par; coupon > yield => price above par. Price and yield are inversely related.
$y \approx [C + (F-P)/n] / [(F+P)/2]$ - coupon plus annualized capital gain, over average of face and price.
